name: Monaco
summary: A tiny principality on the French Riviera ruled by the Grimaldi family since 1297, under French, Spanish or Sardinian protection for long periods; independent by treaty with France (1861). Famous for its casino and Grand Prix.

location.value: French Riviera; about 2.08 km², the second-smallest sovereign state.

terrain.value: A narrow strip of rocky coast below the Maritime Alps, with the Rock of Monaco headland; much land is reclaimed from the sea, as at Fontvieille.

climate.value: Mediterranean: mild, wet winters and hot, dry summers, sheltered from northern winds by the mountains.

resources.value: Few natural resources: the harbour and, until 1848, lemons and olives from Menton and Roquebrune; today its wealth comes from tourism, banking and property.

disasters.value: Occasional storms and coastal flooding; earthquakes have struck the Riviera, notably the Ligurian earthquake of 1887.

urbanisation.value: Entirely urban: one continuous city-state with districts such as Monaco-Ville on the Rock, La Condamine, Monte Carlo and Fontvieille.

disease.value: Plague hit the Riviera in earlier centuries; today residents have one of the world’s highest life expectancies.

migration.value: Foreign residents, especially French and Italians and wealthy people from many countries drawn by low taxes, far outnumber Monégasque citizens.

economicBase.value: Tourism is a main source of income; the Grand Casino opened in 1858; banking holds over €100 billion in funds; Monaco has never levied income tax on individuals.

tradeRoutes.value: Customs union with its larger neighbour.

wealth.value: One of the richest places in the world per person; it struggled after losing Menton and Roquebrune in 1848, until the Monte Carlo casino opened (1863).

moneyAndTax.value: Euro; no personal income tax, except for French citizens.

inequality.value: Very wealthy residents live alongside many workers who commute daily from France and Italy because housing is so expensive.

governmentType.value: The infobox says semi-constitutional monarchy, while the text says it has been a constitutional monarchy since the 1911 constitution (adopted 5 January 1911).

keyRulers.value: The House of Grimaldi has ruled since 1297 with brief interruptions. Rainier III reigned from 1949 until 2005 (he handed his duties to his son on 31 March 2005 and died six days later); Albert II is head of state. Charles III is not covered in the part read.

succession.value: Hereditary in the House of Grimaldi; a 1918 treaty with France aimed to keep the throne in the family and out of foreign hands.

institutions.value: National Council; the 1911 Constitution (5 January 1911), adopted under pressure.

stability.value: Largely stable for centuries; the 1910 revolution led to the 1911 constitution, and a 1959–62 crisis to the 1962 constitution.

eliteConflict.value: Rare: disputes between princes and the National Council, as in 1959 when Rainier III suspended the constitution, ended in compromise.

armyAndTech.value: Ceremonial guards; defence by its neighbour.

majorWars.value: Occupied by Italy in 1943, then by Germany after Italy’s fall (September 1943).

territoryChange.value: Lost most of its land when Menton and Roquebrune broke away in 1848 and were sold to France in 1861; it has since grown by land reclamation.

alliancesRivals.value: Under Spanish protection (1524–1641), then French; under treaties of 1861 and 1918, France guarantees its independence and defence.

inventions.value: No major inventions, but Prince Albert I founded the Oceanographic Museum (opened 1910), a centre for marine science.

scienceEducation.value: State schools follow the French curriculum; the International University of Monaco teaches business, and the Oceanographic Museum supports marine research.

openness.value: Very open: an open border with France, use of the euro, and many foreign residents, businesses and visitors.

communicationTransport.value: A harbour at La Condamine, a station on the French coastal railway (opened 1868), buses and public lifts; the nearest airport is Nice.

religion.value: Catholicism is official: 82.3% Catholic and 86.0% Christian.

languageWriting.value: French is the official language; Monégasque, a Ligurian dialect close to Genoese, is taught in schools, and Italian and English are widely spoken.

artsArchitecture.value: The Belle Époque casino and opera house (Salle Garnier, 1879) by Charles Garnier, Ballets Russes seasons from 1911, and the Prince’s Palace.

socialStructure.value: Monégasques are 24.1% of residents (2024); fewer than 10,000 are Monégasque nationals.

sharedIdentity.value: Pride in the Grimaldi dynasty, the Monégasque language and festivals such as Saint Devote’s day (27 January) and National Day (19 November).

dailyLife.value: Most people live in apartment blocks; local dishes include barbagiuan (fried pastries) and socca, and many workers commute from France.

neighbours.value: Surrounded on land by France (the Alpes-Maritimes department), with Italy a few kilometres east along the coast.

ideasReligions.value: Catholicism as the state religion, Albert I’s support for ocean science and conservation, and the Grimaldis’ patronage of the arts.

colonisation.value: Recognised as sovereign by France in 1641; occupied by revolutionary France 1793–1814; a Sardinian protectorate 1815–1860.

riseSignals.value: The Grimaldi family took the fortress in 1297 disguised as Franciscan friars; Le Grand Casino opened in 1858.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; its modern rise began with the Monte Carlo casino (1863) and grew under Rainier III (1949–2005).

declineSignals.value: No clear decline; its main setback was losing Menton and Roquebrune (1848–61), which removed most of its land and income.

outcome.value: Still in existence as a sovereign principality ruled by the Grimaldi family, closely tied to France.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
